content: Addressing gaps in data collection and reporting systems can significantly aid in the development of effective investment plans. For example, Uganda's paper-based tuberculosis (TB) surveillance system demonstrates the importance of monitoring and validating data. In 2011, all 468 expected district reports were successfully submitted to the national level, meeting the reporting standard for that year. This achievement highlights the emphasis placed on monitoring and validating reports within Uganda's National Tuberculosis Program (NTP). In Uganda, the Basic Management Unit (BMU) is defined at the district level, and facilities within the NTP, along with private clinics and hospitals, contribute to the TB surveillance network. Quarterly aggregate reports from districts are sent to the national level through Zonal TB and Leprosy Supervisors (ZTLSs), who validate the data before forwarding it. These reports are routinely reviewed during quarterly zonal meetings, which involve district TB and leprosy supervisors, laboratory personnel, administrative officers, and other key stakeholders. Some innovative districts also hold quarterly meetings at the district level, involving sub-county health workers and nurses responsible for diagnostic treatment units. Standard operating procedures (SOPs) for submitting data to the national database require provinces to include data from all sub-provincial providers before submission. The NTP also receives quarterly data from the prison service and a non-governmental organization (NGO) providing TB diagnostic and treatment services outside the NTP. In 2011, 47 out of 48 expected data files were received, representing 98% compliance. However, one province failed to submit data for the fourth quarter, partially meeting the standard. The results showed that all provinces, the prison service, and the NGO reported cases in each quarter, except for one province that did not report any cases in the fourth quarter. This indicates a missing data file in the national database. The World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines emphasize the use of standardized recording and reporting forms for TB case registration. These forms collect patient demographic and clinical data, as well as sputum examination results, to monitor treatment progress. Data from these forms are consolidated at the BMU level to produce quarterly reports, which feed into nationwide reports. These reports provide insights into the TB burden and the performance of the surveillance system. However, inaccurate or incomplete data compilation at the BMU level can lead to erroneous conclusions. To assess data quality, the Service Availability and Readiness Assessment (SARA) tool, developed by WHO and USAID, is recommended. This tool evaluates the availability of key resources, equipment, medicines, and diagnostic capacities in health facilities. Repeat assessments using SARA can track progress in health system strengthening over time. The SARA methodology involves visits to BMUs and their respective health facilities, with data collected through key informant interviews and document reviews. Sampling methodologies, such as Lot Quality Assurance Sampling (LQAS), are used to determine the number of BMUs to be assessed. This approach requires a thorough understanding of the TB surveillance system structure, as BMU types vary between countries. In smaller countries, all BMUs may need to be included in the assessment. Data quality assessments involve verifying the consistency and completeness of data across various sources, such as BMU TB registers, laboratory registers, and patient treatment cards. For example, the number of cases reported in BMU quarterly reports should match the data in TB registers and laboratory records. Electronic recording and reporting systems are recommended to overcome the limitations of paper-based systems. These systems enable automated validation checks during data entry and subsequent database queries, improving data quality. National guidelines for recording and reporting should be updated to reflect these benchmarks. When benchmarks are not met, corrective actions such as training and strengthening monitoring and evaluation (M&E) processes should be implemented. Countries should consider transitioning to electronic systems to enhance data quality and reliability. Additionally, investment plans should include estimated budgets to address gaps and achieve data quality standards. In summary, ensuring accurate, complete, and consistent data is critical for effective TB surveillance and program management. Transitioning to electronic systems and adhering to standardized guidelines can significantly improve data quality, enabling reliable assessments of TB incidence and program performance.
